text: Before you can allocate a single qubit, you need somewhere for Q# code to actually compile and run. Unlike Qiskit, where pip install qiskit gets you most of the way there, Q# has two genuinely different entry points, and picking the right one matters for how the rest of this course will feel.

The first is a standalone dot-q-s project driven by VS Code. You install the Azure Quantum Development Kit extension, and it gives your files syntax highlighting, real-time type checking, and a Run code lens that appears directly above any operation marked EntryPoint. The second is Python or Jupyter, through the qsharp package — you write Q# into a percent-percent-qsharp notebook cell, or pass Q# source strings into qsharp.eval or qsharp.run from Python. Both paths compile the exact same language — you're not learning two dialects, just two different harnesses around the same compiler. The qsharp-widgets package becomes required later, for rendering resource-estimate reports right inside a notebook.

For the Python and Jupyter path, setup is one command: pip install qsharp qsharp-widgets. The VS Code path doesn't need this at all — that extension bundles its own compiler, no separate dot-NET SDK or Python install required.

A standalone Q# project is just a folder with two things: a small JSON manifest named qsharp-dot-json at the root, whose presence tells the VS Code extension this folder is a Q# project, and a src directory holding your dot-q-s files, conventionally starting with Main-dot-qs. Inside it, every runnable program needs exactly one operation marked EntryPoint — that's what the Run code lens and the compiler look for as the program's starting point.

Everything you just saw runs entirely on your own machine, against the QDK's built-in simulator — no Azure account, subscription, or workspace involved yet. You'll meet two simulator flavors by name later: a sparse-state simulator, efficient for programs with limited entanglement, and a full-state simulator, exact, but its memory cost doubles with every additional qubit. For now, local simulation is simply the default, zero-setup way to check a program compiles and behaves as expected, before any Azure Quantum resource estimation or hardware submission enters the picture.
Next lesson, the classical skeleton every Q# program is built on: namespaces, the operation-versus-function split, typed bindings, and control flow.
